state:
The Linden Street community garden opened in the spring with forty raised beds, a tool shed and two rain barrels. Members pay a small yearly fee that covers water, compost and the insurance policy the city requires. Each member agrees to work four hours a month on shared tasks such as turning the compost, weeding the paths and repairing the fence along the alley. A volunteer committee of five people meets on the first Tuesday of every month to review applications, plan workdays and settle disagreements about plot boundaries.

In June the committee noticed that the north rain barrel had cracked near its base. Water leaked onto the gravel path and formed a puddle that froze twice during a cold week. One member proposed replacing both barrels with a single larger tank, while another suggested repairing the crack with a marine sealant that costs about twelve dollars. The treasurer reported that the garden had three hundred and ten dollars left in its maintenance budget for the year.

Plot 17 has been unused since April. Its holder, who moved to another city, did not answer two letters and one phone message. The waiting list has eleven names on it; the first person on the list has been waiting since last October and lives two blocks away. The bylaws say that a plot left unplanted for ninety days may be reassigned after one written notice, and that the notice must give the holder fourteen days to reply.

The tool shed lock was replaced in July after a set of pruning shears and a wheelbarrow went missing. New keys were given to every member who signed the updated agreement. Four members have not yet collected their keys, and two of them have asked whether the code lock that a neighbouring garden uses would be cheaper over five years. A code lock costs about ninety dollars, and copying a key costs four dollars each time.

During the August heat wave the garden used more water than in any previous month. The water bill was one hundred and forty dollars, almost twice the usual amount. Several members watered in the middle of the afternoon, when much of the water evaporates. The committee drafted a notice asking members to water before nine in the morning or after six in the evening, and to use the soaker hoses stored in the shed instead of the spray nozzles.

A local school asked whether its after-school club could use two of the empty beds for a pumpkin project in the autumn. The club has twelve children and two teachers, and it would visit on Wednesday afternoons. Some members welcomed the idea; others worried about noise, about children walking through planted beds, and about who would be responsible if a child was hurt by a tool. The insurance policy covers volunteers but does not mention visitors.

At the September meeting the committee voted on three motions. The first, to reassign plot 17, passed four to one. The second, to buy a code lock, was postponed until the treasurer could compare prices. The third, to let the school club use two beds for one season on a trial basis, passed three to two, on the condition that a teacher is present at every visit and that the children stay on the marked paths.

The harvest festival is planned for the second Saturday of October. Members will bring dishes made with produce from their plots, and the committee will set up two tables near the gate. Last year the festival drew about sixty people from the neighbourhood, and three of them later joined the waiting list. This year the committee hopes to raise money for a new compost bin by selling seedlings and asking for small donations.

questions.instr: May plot 17 be reassigned under the bylaws once notice has been given?
What happened to the code-lock motion?
Under what condition may the school club use the beds?
options: a teacher is present at every visit and children stay on the paths
the club pays the yearly fee

questions.instr: When should members water?
How much remained in the maintenance budget?
Rate how contentious the committee's year was.
